title: The: General Ideas and Specific Groups
summary: Choose between no article and the when discussing people, objects and ideas in general or identifying a particular group, quantity or instance. Notice that a descriptive phrase does not always make a noun specific.
learningObjectives: Use plural nouns and uncountable nouns without the for general statements and preferences.
Use the with nouns made identifiable by a shared context or a specifying phrase.
Distinguish general categories with descriptive modifiers from specific individuals or groups.
Use most before a general plural noun without adding the, and recognise when a particular set is intended.

explanation.heading: General plurals and uncountable ideas
explanation.body: To talk about a whole category, usually use a plural noun without an article: cyclists, keyboards or neighbours. Uncountable nouns can also represent a general idea without an article, as in music, information and patience. The speaker is not pointing to particular individuals or a particular amount. This applies to general likes, habits, facts and opinions.
explanation.example: Cyclists need reliable lights, and patience helps on busy roads.

explanation.heading: The identifies a particular set or instance
explanation.body: Add the when the listener can identify which people or things you mean. A relative clause, an earlier mention or the immediate situation can establish that identity: the cyclists waiting at this crossing, the documents on my desk or the information in yesterday’s email. With uncountable nouns, the can single out a particular portion or instance without changing the noun into a countable one.
explanation.example: The cyclists waiting outside the café have left their helmets by the door.

explanation.heading: A modifier can still describe a general category
explanation.body: An adjective or a relative clause does not automatically require the. Compare people who enjoy puzzles (anyone fitting the description) with the people in our interview group (a known set). Similarly, fresh bread or quiet libraries can refer generally to types of bread or libraries. Ask whether the phrase describes a kind of thing or points to identifiable members of a group.
explanation.example: People who travel frequently often look for flexible tickets.

explanation.heading: Contrast general preferences with particular experiences
explanation.body: Food, art, weather, transport and other broad subjects usually have no the when they describe personal tastes or general topics. Use the if your opinion concerns a clearly identified instance: the food at the conference, the art in this room or the transport arranged for our visitors. A shared occasion can make a noun identifiable even when it has not been mentioned earlier.
explanation.example: I enjoy live music, but the music at last night’s event was too loud.

explanation.heading: Most with general plurals
explanation.body: Use most + plural noun for a general majority: most passengers, most offices, most children. Do not add the between most and the noun in this pattern. The most is used in different constructions, including superlatives, but not as a replacement for most in these general statements. A phrase such as the passengers on our bus identifies a particular set rather than passengers generally.
explanation.example: Most passengers prefer direct trains, but the passengers on today’s shuttle requested an extra stop.

comparisons.title: A category in general versus an identified group

left.label: No article: category
left.example: Designers often work with tight deadlines.
left.note: The statement concerns designers as a general group.

right.label: The: identified members
right.example: The designers on this project work remotely.
right.note: The phrase on this project points to a particular group.

comparisons.title: Uncountable ideas in general versus one occasion

left.label: No article: general idea
left.note: Coffee and sugar are types of drink and ingredient generally.

right.label: The: particular serving
right.example: The coffee at breakfast was too strong.
right.note: At breakfast identifies a specific serving or occasion.

examples.sentence: Old photographs can reveal how a neighbourhood has changed.
examples.note: Old photographs is a broad category, not a particular collection.

examples.sentence: The photographs we found in the attic were badly damaged.
examples.note: The relative clause identifies one collection.

examples.sentence: Students who speak several languages may notice patterns across them.
examples.note: The relative clause still defines a general category of students.

examples.sentence: The students in our workshop have already received their certificates.
examples.note: Our workshop identifies the relevant group of students.

examples.sentence: Most restaurants publish menus online, but the menu at this restaurant has not been updated.
examples.note: Most restaurants makes a general claim; the menu refers to one specific restaurant.

commonMistakes.incorrect: In general, the smartphones need charging regularly.
commonMistakes.correct: In general, smartphones need charging regularly.
commonMistakes.why: The sentence discusses smartphones as a category rather than identified devices.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please return books you borrowed from my office yesterday.
commonMistakes.correct: Please return the books you borrowed from my office yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: The relative clause identifies a particular set of books.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I love the jazz in general.
commonMistakes.why: A musical genre discussed generally is uncountable and has no article.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The most visitors arrive before the museum opens.
commonMistakes.correct: Most visitors arrive before the museum opens.
commonMistakes.why: Most before a general plural noun does not take the.

studyTips: Before choosing an article, label each noun as a general category or something the listener can identify.
Create paired examples with the same noun: books are useful / the books in this bag are useful.
Pay attention to the difference between a category description (people who cook at home) and a particular group (the people at our table).

exercises.prompt: Speaking about animals in general, ___ often recognise familiar voices.
exercises.feedback: A general statement about dogs as a category takes the plural Dogs without an article.

exercises.prompt: I bought some milk for tonight. Please put ___ in the fridge.
exercises.feedback: The milk is identifiable from the earlier mention of a particular purchase.

exercises.prompt: A colleague says: “I enjoy outdoor concerts, but the concert we attended yesterday was disappointing.” What does “the concert” refer to?
choices: Concerts as a type of entertainment.
exercises.feedback: The concert identifies the shared event from yesterday, unlike concerts as a general category.

exercises.prompt: In general, ___ appreciate clear instructions on their first day.
exercises.feedback: Use most + plural noun for a general majority: most employees.

exercises.prompt: I enjoy ___ (art form in general; write the one-word uncountable noun: music).
exercises.feedback: Music without the means music as a general category, not one particular performance.

exercises.prompt: ___ (the bicycles stored in our garage; write the article and plural noun) need new tyres.
exercises.feedback: A particular set of bicycles is identified by its location in our garage.

exercises.prompt: ___ (people in general; write the plural noun for people) sometimes underestimate travel times.
exercises.feedback: People as a general group does not take the.

exercises.prompt: I could not follow ___ (the instructions in the email you sent; write the article and noun).
exercises.feedback: The message identifies a particular set of instructions.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: In general, the cats are curious animals.
acceptedAnswers: In general, cats are curious animals.
exercises.feedback: The broad generalisation refers to cats as a species, so omit the.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Please review figures we discussed at yesterday’s meeting.
acceptedAnswers: Please review the figures we discussed at yesterday’s meeting.
exercises.feedback: The specifying clause identifies a particular set of figures, so include the.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The most tourists visit the old town on foot.
acceptedAnswers: Most tourists visit the old town on foot.
exercises.feedback: Most + a general plural noun does not take the.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I appreciate the honesty in general.
exercises.feedback: Honesty is an abstract uncountable idea here, not an identifiable instance.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one general statement using exactly these facts: bicycles; need regular maintenance. Begin with “Bicycles”.
speakingExercises.feedback: A plural noun naming a category does not need the.

speakingExercises.prompt: Now refer to a particular set: the bicycles outside the workshop; need repairs. Begin with “The bicycles”.
acceptedAnswers: The bicycles outside the workshop need repairs.
speakingExercises.feedback: Outside the workshop identifies the relevant bicycles, so use the.

speakingExercises.prompt: A speaker likes music generally, but finds the music at this restaurant too loud. Use one sentence starting “I like” and join the ideas with “but”.
acceptedAnswers: I like music, but the music at this restaurant is too loud.
speakingExercises.feedback: Music is general in the first clause; the music at this restaurant is a specific instance.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a general majority statement from these exact facts: most visitors; arrive before noon. Begin with “Most”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Most visitors is the normal pattern for a general majority.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one complete sentence using these facts: a group of workers in our department; has finished training. Begin with “The workers”.
acceptedAnswers: The workers in our department have finished training.
speakingExercises.feedback: Our department identifies a particular group, and workers takes have.

speakingExercises.prompt: A guest asks which water to replace. Facts: the water in this bottle is warm. Say one sentence beginning “The water”.
acceptedAnswers: The water in this bottle is warm.
speakingExercises.feedback: The water identifies the contents of a particular bottle.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the article use and say the whole sentence: “I enjoy the coffee in general.” Change only what is necessary.
speakingExercises.feedback: Coffee is a general uncountable category here, so omit the.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make exactly two sentences. First give a general fact: books can be expensive. Then identify a set: the books on that shelf belong to Lina. Begin with “Books” and “The books”.
acceptedAnswers: Books can be expensive. The books on that shelf belong to Lina.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first sentence is about books as a category; the second points to a specific set.

listeningExercises.audioText: Storms do not usually bother me, but the storm last night kept me awake for hours.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker distinguishes storms generally from the storm on one specific night.

listeningExercises.audioText: Most customers use our digital menu, but the customers at table six asked for printed copies.
listeningExercises.feedback: The customers at table six refers to a specific set, unlike most customers.

listeningExercises.audioText: The documents you requested are on the reception desk.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the first two words you hear, including the article.
listeningExercises.feedback: The documents is a specific set identified by you requested.

listeningExercises.audioText: I usually enjoy spicy food, but the curry we ordered yesterday was far too hot for me.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which statement best describes the speaker’s opinion?
choices: They generally like spicy food but disliked one particular curry.
They liked yesterday’s curry more than usual.
listeningExercises.feedback: Spicy food is the general category; the curry we ordered yesterday is one specific dish.

listeningExercises.audioText: I do not usually drink juice. Could you move the juice beside your laptop away from these papers?
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker want moved?
choices: A particular juice container near the laptop.
listeningExercises.feedback: The juice beside your laptop identifies a particular item, not juice as a general drink.

listeningExercises.audioText: Bees help plants produce seeds, but the bees in our courtyard have disappeared this summer.
listeningExercises.prompt: What specific change concerns the speaker?
choices: The plants have all stopped growing.
The bees in their courtyard are no longer there.
listeningExercises.feedback: Bees is the broad group in the first clause; the bees in our courtyard identifies the affected group.

listeningExercises.audioText: Most people learn better when they have time to practise new skills.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the first two words of the audio.
listeningExercises.feedback: Most people identifies a general majority without the.

listeningExercises.audioText: Please check the figures in the final table before we send the report.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word noun phrase immediately after “check”.
listeningExercises.feedback: The figures identifies the numbers in a particular table.
